questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: infant under 1 excluding newborn
questions.text: AHA Part 1 defines an 'infant' for BLS purposes. Which definition matches?

answers.text: From age 1 through puberty
Younger than 6 months only
Birth through age 5
Younger than 1 year, excluding newly born infants in the delivery room

explanations.a: From 1 year to puberty defines a child, not an infant.
explanations.b: The infant category extends through the entire first year of life, not just the first 6 months.
explanations.c: Birth through age 5 spans both infant and child categories.
explanations.d: AHA Part 1 defines an infant as someone younger than 1 year, excluding newly born infants in the delivery room.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: pediatric arrest respiratory cause oxygen content
questions.text: AHA Part 6 explains why pediatric CPR must include both compressions and breaths. Which physiologic reason does the manual cite?

answers.text: Children's hearts cannot generate any electrical activity
Pediatric cardiac arrests are commonly due to respiratory causes, so blood oxygen content is already reduced before arrest
Children always have shorter resuscitation times than adults
Compression-only CPR is unsafe for any age group

explanations.a: Children's hearts can have shockable rhythms; the rationale is about oxygen content, not electrical activity.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 explains that infant and child arrests are commonly due to respiratory causes, so oxygen content is reduced before arrest and compressions alone do not deliver oxygenated blood as effectively as compressions plus breaths.
explanations.c: Resuscitation duration is not the AHA-cited rationale for breaths in pediatric CPR.
explanations.d: Compression-only CPR is recommended for untrained adult lay rescuers; it is not unsafe, just suboptimal for pediatrics.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: puberty signs treat as adult hair breast
questions.text: You are caring for a 14-year-old who has visible chest hair and is in cardiac arrest. According to AHA Part 1, which BLS approach applies?

answers.text: Wait for parental consent before any care
Treat as an adult because there are signs of puberty
Use neonatal resuscitation guidelines
Use pediatric BLS based on chronologic age

explanations.a: Cardiac arrest care is provided under implied consent; waiting for parental consent delays critical treatment.
explanations.b: AHA Part 1 lists chest or underarm hair on males and any breast development on females as signs of puberty, after which BLS treats the patient as an adult.
explanations.c: Neonatal guidelines apply to the newly born in the delivery room, not adolescents.
explanations.d: AHA defines the adult range as starting at puberty, regardless of chronologic age below 18.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: child 1 to puberty definition
questions.text: Which range does AHA Part 1 use to define a 'child' for pediatric BLS?

answers.text: From birth to age 2
Anyone younger than 18 regardless of physical development
From age 6 to age 12 only
From 1 year of age to puberty

explanations.a: Birth to age 2 includes infants and only the youngest children, not the full child range.
explanations.b: Adolescents who have reached puberty are treated as adults under BLS, not as children.
explanations.c: Restricting to ages 6-12 excludes younger children covered by pediatric BLS.
explanations.d: AHA Part 1 defines a child as anyone from 1 year of age to the onset of puberty.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: step 1 verify scene safety
questions.text: An infant lies motionless on a kitchen floor. According to Step 1 of the AHA Pediatric BLS Single-Rescuer Sequence, what is the rescuer's very first action?

answers.text: Verify that the scene is safe for the rescuer and the infant
Apply AED pads before reaching the infant
Begin chest compressions immediately
Wait for a second rescuer to arrive before doing anything

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 makes Step 1 of the pediatric sequence an explicit scene safety verification.
explanations.b: AED pads can only be placed after the rescuer is at the child's side with the AED ready.
explanations.c: Compressions cannot be provided until the rescuer has reached the child and confirmed cardiac arrest.
explanations.d: Waiting for parents wastes minutes when a child's brain is failing.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: unwitnessed no device 5 cycles then activate
questions.text: You are alone with an unresponsive 8-month-old whose collapse you did not witness, and you have no mobile device. According to the AHA Pediatric BLS Single-Rescuer Sequence, what should you do before leaving to activate EMS?

answers.text: Perform 5 cycles or about 2 minutes of CPR first
Provide breaths only and never give compressions
Leave immediately to call for help
Wait for the parents before starting any care

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 directs the lone rescuer at an unwitnessed pediatric collapse without a mobile device to perform 5 cycles or about 2 minutes of CPR before leaving to activate EMS and get an AED.
explanations.b: Compressions are essential; pediatric CPR requires both compressions and breaths.
explanations.c: Leaving an unwitnessed pediatric arrest before any CPR omits the most important early intervention for a respiratory-cause arrest.
explanations.d: Waiting for parents wastes minutes during which oxygen delivery to the brain is failing.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: witnessed sudden collapse lone leave get AED return
questions.text: You are alone with a 5-year-old you saw suddenly collapse, and no mobile device is available. According to the AHA Pediatric Single-Rescuer Sequence, what is the correct action?

answers.text: Remain beside the child and hope someone walks by
Continue checking responsiveness every minute and do nothing else
Provide 30 minutes of CPR before any activation
Leave the child to activate EMS and get an AED, then return to perform CPR

explanations.a: Doing nothing while waiting wastes minutes during which the brain is being deprived of oxygen.
explanations.b: Repeated responsiveness checks without action do not address cardiac arrest.
explanations.c: An indefinite delay before activation contradicts the witnessed-collapse rule and lowers survival.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 directs a lone rescuer who witnessed a child's sudden collapse to leave to activate EMS and get an AED, then return to perform CPR.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: single rescuer 30 to 2 child infant
questions.text: When you begin CPR alone on an unresponsive child or infant, what compression-to-ventilation ratio does AHA Part 6 specify for a single rescuer?

answers.text: 30 compressions to 2 breaths
15 compressions to 2 breaths
5 compressions to 1 breath
Continuous compressions with no breaths

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 says the compression-to-ventilation ratio for single rescuers is 30:2 in adults, children, and infants.
explanations.b: The 15:2 ratio applies when 2 or more rescuers provide CPR to a child or infant, not when a single rescuer is alone.
explanations.c: 5:1 is not part of any current AHA recommendation.
explanations.d: Pediatric CPR includes breaths because the arrest is most often respiratory in origin.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: AED use as soon as available pediatric
questions.text: While performing CPR alone on a child, you finally retrieve the AED. AHA Part 6 directs you to do what with the device?

answers.text: Wait until 5 full cycles of CPR are completed before turning it on
Use the AED as soon as it is available
Use it only if the child does not regain a pulse after 10 minutes
Avoid using an AED on any child

explanations.a: Delaying AED use after retrieval contradicts the principle of early defibrillation.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 directs rescuers to use the AED as soon as it is available during pediatric resuscitation.
explanations.c: Survival drops with every minute of arrest; waiting 10 minutes is not part of the algorithm.
explanations.d: AEDs are absolutely indicated for children; pediatric pads or attenuators are used when available.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: first rescuer stays second activates retrieves
questions.text: Two rescuers simultaneously discover an unresponsive infant. According to the AHA Pediatric BLS Multirescuer Sequence, how should the two divide initial tasks?

answers.text: Both rescuers leave to call for help, then return
The second rescuer alone performs all initial assessment and care
Both rescuers stand back and wait for paramedics
The first rescuer remains with the infant while the second activates EMS and retrieves the AED

explanations.a: Both rescuers leaving the infant abandons the patient; one must stay to provide care.
explanations.b: Splitting tasks effectively means both rescuers are working — one stays and provides care while the other activates and retrieves equipment.
explanations.c: Standing back during pediatric arrest is never the multirescuer plan.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 explicitly directs the first rescuer to remain with the infant or child while the second rescuer activates EMS and retrieves the AED.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: ratio changes to 15 to 2 when second arrives
questions.text: You begin pediatric CPR alone using a 30:2 ratio. When the second rescuer returns, AHA Part 6 directs the team to switch to which ratio?

answers.text: Switch to continuous compressions with no breaths
Switch to 15 compressions to 2 breaths
Continue at 30:2 until ALS arrives
Switch to 50 compressions to 1 breath

explanations.a: Continuous compressions without breaths is for adults with an advanced airway, not pediatric 2-rescuer BLS.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 specifies 15:2 when 2 or more rescuers work on an infant or child, prioritizing ventilation because pediatric arrests are commonly respiratory in origin.
explanations.c: Continuing 30:2 with two rescuers misses the AHA-recommended pediatric ratio change.
explanations.d: 50:1 is not part of any current AHA recommendation.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: 15 to 2 rationale respiratory cause ventilation priority
questions.text: AHA Part 6 gives a specific physiologic reason for using 15:2 instead of 30:2 when 2 rescuers work on a child or infant. What is that reason?

answers.text: It prioritizes ventilation because pediatric arrests are commonly due to respiratory causes
It reduces the rescuer's fatigue without affecting the patient
It allows the AED to charge faster
It is required by state law in most U.S. jurisdictions

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 explains that 15:2 prioritizes ventilation because pediatric arrests are commonly due to respiratory causes.
explanations.b: Rescuer fatigue is real but is not the AHA rationale for the ratio change.
explanations.c: AED charging speed is independent of compression-to-ventilation ratio.
explanations.d: AHA guidelines drive the ratio choice rather than state law.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: shockable rhythm 1 shock then CPR 2 minutes
questions.text: During pediatric resuscitation, the AED prompts that a shockable rhythm is detected. According to the AHA Pediatric BLS Multirescuer Sequence, what should the team do after delivering the shock?

answers.text: Pause for 5 minutes to allow recovery
Stop CPR until the child shows spontaneous movement
Immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes until the AED prompts another rhythm check
Check the pulse for at least 60 seconds before resuming care

explanations.a: A 5-minute pause would abandon the resuscitation entirely during a critical window.
explanations.b: Stopping CPR after a shock is the opposite of the algorithm direction; immediate resumption maintains perfusion.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 directs the team to immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes after a shock, until the AED prompts another rhythm check.
explanations.d: 60-second post-shock pulse checks contradict AHA timing and delay restart of compressions.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: continue until PALS or reacts breathing moves
questions.text: AHA Part 6 says rescuers should continue the CPR-AED cycle during pediatric resuscitation until one of two conditions is met. What are those conditions?

answers.text: Until 5 cycles are completed or 10 minutes have passed
Until the AED battery dies or the family asks for a stop
Until PALS professionals take over or the infant or child begins to breathe, move, or otherwise react
Until the rescuer becomes too tired to continue

explanations.a: There is no AHA-stipulated time-out at 5 cycles or 10 minutes; care continues until PALS or response.
explanations.b: Battery death and family requests are practical issues but not the AHA-defined stopping criteria.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 says continue until PALS professionals take over or the infant or child begins to breathe, move, or otherwise react.
explanations.d: Rescuer fatigue is addressed by switching compressors, not by stopping care.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: single rescuer same 30 to 2 all ages
questions.text: An instructor compares single-rescuer compression-to-ventilation ratios across adults, children, and infants. Which statement is consistent with AHA Part 6?

answers.text: Adults are 30:2; children are 15:2; infants are 5:1
Adults are continuous; children are 30:2; infants are 15:2
The single-rescuer ratio is 30:2 for adults, children, and infants alike
Adults are 15:2; children are 15:2; infants are 5:1

explanations.a: Children and infants use 30:2 for a single rescuer, not 15:2 and 5:1.
explanations.b: Continuous compressions without breaths apply only after advanced airway placement, not as the default ratio.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 says the single-rescuer compression-to-ventilation ratio is the same — 30:2 — in adults, children, and infants.
explanations.d: Adults at 15:2 contradicts AHA guidance; the adult ratio is 30:2.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: advanced airway pediatric 20 to 30 breaths per minute
questions.text: A pediatric advanced airway is placed during a child's resuscitation. AHA's high-quality CPR component table specifies which ventilation strategy after advanced airway placement?

answers.text: Continuous compressions at 100 to 120 per minute and 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds
Pause compressions to give 2 breaths every 15 compressions
Stop ventilations once the airway is placed
Continuous compressions at 60 per minute and 1 breath every 2 seconds

explanations.a: AHA's high-quality CPR table for children and infants with an advanced airway calls for continuous compressions at 100 to 120 per minute with 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds — 20 to 30 breaths per minute.
explanations.b: Pausing compressions for breaths defeats the purpose of an advanced airway.
explanations.c: Ventilations remain essential after an advanced airway is placed.
explanations.d: 60 per minute is below the AHA-specified compression rate.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: respiratory arrest with pulse 1 breath 2 to 3 seconds
questions.text: An infant has abnormal breathing but a definite pulse is felt. According to AHA Part 6 Step 3b, what breath rate should the rescuer provide?

answers.text: 1 breath every 6 seconds or 10 breaths per minute
1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds or 20 to 30 breaths per minute
1 breath every 10 seconds or 6 breaths per minute
No breaths until cardiac arrest is confirmed

explanations.a: Ten breaths per minute is the adult rate after advanced airway placement, not the pediatric ventilatory support rate.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 Step 3b specifies 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds or 20 to 30 breaths per minute when an infant or child has abnormal breathing but a pulse.
explanations.c: Six breaths per minute is below the AHA pediatric range for ventilatory support.
explanations.d: Withholding breaths until full arrest contradicts the algorithm; respiratory failure with a pulse calls for immediate ventilation.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: 5 cycles 2 minutes approximate duration
questions.text: How long does approximately 5 cycles of single-rescuer 30:2 pediatric CPR take, per the AHA Part 6 reference used in algorithm steps?

answers.text: About 30 seconds
About 10 minutes
About 2 minutes
About 30 minutes

explanations.a: Thirty seconds is far too short for 5 full 30:2 cycles.
explanations.b: Ten minutes overstates the time required by a factor of five.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 references about 2 minutes for 5 cycles of 30:2 CPR.
explanations.d: Thirty minutes overstates the time required for 5 cycles by an order of magnitude.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: 15 to 2 two rescuer peds vs 30 to 2 adult
questions.text: A student asks why pediatric 2-rescuer CPR uses 15:2 while adult 2-rescuer CPR still uses 30:2. Which AHA rationale directly explains the pediatric difference?

answers.text: Pediatric patients have smaller hands so they need fewer compressions
State regulations require 15:2 for all patients under 12
Pediatric arrests are commonly due to respiratory causes, so ventilation is prioritized by doubling the relative breath frequency
The 15:2 ratio is easier for rescuers to remember than 30:2

explanations.a: Hand size does not determine the compression-to-ventilation ratio.
explanations.b: State regulations do not set the ratio; AHA guidelines do.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 specifies 15:2 for 2-rescuer pediatric CPR because pediatric arrests are commonly due to respiratory causes and ventilation must be prioritized.
explanations.d: Simplicity of recall is not the clinical rationale.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: infant depth 4 cm one third AP
questions.text: When performing chest compressions on an infant in cardiac arrest, what depth does AHA Part 6 specify?

answers.text: At least 2 inches (5 cm) regardless of body size
At least 3 inches (7.5 cm)
Less than half an inch to avoid injury
At least one third the AP diameter of the chest, approximately 1 1/2 inches (4 cm)

explanations.a: Two inches is the adult depth, not the infant depth, and would be excessive on an infant chest.
explanations.b: Three inches is far beyond the AHA-specified infant depth.
explanations.c: Compressing less than half an inch fails to generate adequate cardiac output.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 specifies infant compressions of at least one third the AP diameter of the chest, approximately 1 1/2 inches or 4 cm.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: child depth 5 cm one third AP
questions.text: When performing chest compressions on a 6-year-old in cardiac arrest, what depth does AHA Part 6 specify?

answers.text: At least one third the AP diameter of the chest, approximately 2 inches (5 cm)
At least 1 inch (2.5 cm)
At least 4 inches (10 cm)
Exactly 1 1/2 inches (4 cm), the same as an infant

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 specifies child compressions of at least one third the AP diameter of the chest, approximately 2 inches or 5 cm.
explanations.b: One inch falls below the AHA-specified child depth.
explanations.c: Four inches is far beyond the AHA-specified child depth.
explanations.d: Children require deeper compressions than infants because their chests are larger.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: AP diameter fraction scales with size
questions.text: AHA Part 6 expresses pediatric compression depth as 'at least one third the AP diameter' of the chest rather than a fixed measurement. Why is a fraction used for children and infants?

answers.text: It prevents the rescuer from compressing too fast
It removes the need to use compressions at all
It is the same fraction used for adult chests
It accommodates the wide range of pediatric body sizes from infant to adolescent

explanations.a: Compression rate is a separate parameter not tied to depth fractions.
explanations.b: Pediatric CPR absolutely includes compressions; the fraction simply scales depth.
explanations.c: Adult depth is given as a fixed minimum, not a fraction, because adult chest size is more uniform.
explanations.d: Pediatric body size varies dramatically across ages, so AHA expresses depth as a fraction that scales with the patient.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: rate same all ages 100 to 120
questions.text: Which statement about chest compression rate across age groups is consistent with AHA Part 6?

answers.text: Infants need 60 to 80 per minute because they are small
Children need 80 to 100 per minute
The rate is the same — 100 to 120 per minute — for all people in cardiac arrest
Adults need 140 to 160 per minute

explanations.a: Infants receive the same rate as adults; only the depth and hand technique differ.
explanations.b: Children are also compressed at 100 to 120 per minute, not at a slower rate.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 calls 100 to 120 per minute the universal rate for compressions in all people who experience cardiac arrest.
explanations.d: 140 to 160 exceeds the recommended adult range.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: depths compared adult child infant summary
questions.text: AHA Part 6's high-quality CPR component table summarizes compression depths across all age groups. Which set of depths matches?

answers.text: Adults at least 2 inches (5 cm); children at least one third AP diameter approximately 2 inches (5 cm); infants at least one third AP diameter approximately 1 1/2 inches (4 cm)
Adults, children, and infants all at exactly 2 inches (5 cm)
Adults at 3 inches; children at 2.5 inches; infants at 2 inches
Adults at 1 inch; children at 1.5 inches; infants at 2 inches

explanations.a: AHA Part 6's component table lists: adults ≥2 inches (5 cm); children ≥1/3 AP diameter ≈2 inches (5 cm); infants ≥1/3 AP diameter ≈1½ inches (4 cm).
explanations.b: Infant depth is approximately 1½ inches (4 cm), not 2 inches.
explanations.c: These values do not match the AHA component table.
explanations.d: These values invert the correct relationship between adult and infant depths.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: infant heel of 1 hand when cannot encircle
questions.text: You are alone with a choking infant in cardiac arrest. AHA Part 6 recommends which compression technique for a single rescuer who cannot encircle the chest?

answers.text: Use both fists side by side on the upper sternum
Use the heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum
Press laterally on the ribs from one side
Use only the fingertips of one hand on the chest

explanations.a: Two fists on the upper sternum is not a recognized infant technique.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 says if the rescuer cannot encircle the chest, the recommended technique is to compress with the heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum.
explanations.c: Lateral pressure on the ribs does not produce effective central chest compression.
explanations.d: Fingertip-only compression is not the AHA technique; the heel of one hand is preferred when the 2-thumb technique is not feasible.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: infant 2 thumb encircling preferred 2 rescuers
questions.text: Two rescuers are providing CPR to an infant. AHA Part 6 specifies which compression technique is preferred when 2 rescuers are available?

answers.text: The two-handed adult technique on infants
The single fingertip technique
The 2 thumb-encircling hands technique
The fist-on-the-abdomen technique

explanations.a: Two-handed adult technique is too forceful for an infant chest and is not recommended.
explanations.b: Single fingertip technique is not a recognized AHA infant compression method.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 describes the 2 thumb-encircling hands technique as the preferred method when 2 rescuers are available for an infant.
explanations.d: Compressing the abdomen does not generate cardiac output and is not an AHA technique.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: thumbs side by side lower half sternum fingers encircle
questions.text: When using the 2 thumb-encircling hands technique on an infant, where does AHA Part 6 instruct the rescuer to position the thumbs?

answers.text: On the upper sternum just below the clavicles
On the side of the chest along the ribs
Directly over the xiphoid process
Side by side in the center of the chest, on the lower half of the sternum, with fingers encircling the chest

explanations.a: Upper sternum placement near the clavicles produces poor cardiac output.
explanations.b: Lateral rib placement is not AHA technique and will not generate effective compression.
explanations.c: Pressing directly on the xiphoid risks fracturing it and injuring underlying organs.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 instructs thumbs side by side in the center of the chest on the lower half of the sternum, with the hands encircling and supporting the back.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: child 1 or 2 hands achieve depth
questions.text: AHA Part 6 says compressions on a child can be performed with one or two hands. What is the guiding principle for choosing between them?

answers.text: Always use two hands on every child regardless of size
Use only the heel of one hand for children over 8 years
Whichever method achieves at least one third AP-diameter depth, approximately 2 inches (5 cm)
Always use one hand even on adolescents

explanations.a: Two hands are not always required; small children may receive adequate depth with one.
explanations.b: AHA does not restrict children over 8 to one-handed compressions.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 says whether one or two hands is used, the rescuer compresses at least one third the AP diameter approximately 2 inches; the choice is driven by the child's size and the rescuer's strength.
explanations.d: Adolescents who reach puberty are treated as adults and compressed with two hands.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: firm flat surface infant child
questions.text: Before starting compressions on an infant, AHA Part 6 instructs the rescuer to place the infant on a particular type of surface. Which surface is correct?

answers.text: A soft pillow to cushion the back
An inclined surface at 45 degrees
The rescuer's lap if no firm surface is available
A firm, flat surface

explanations.a: A soft pillow absorbs compression force and reduces real chest depression.
explanations.b: An inclined surface complicates compression mechanics.
explanations.c: Compressing on a lap is not an AHA-recommended substitute for a firm flat surface.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 explicitly directs the rescuer to place the infant on a firm, flat surface so compression force translates into actual chest depression.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: infant neck neutral sniffing ear canal shoulder level
questions.text: When opening the airway of an infant, AHA Part 6 emphasizes a specific neck position to maximize an open airway. Which position is described?

answers.text: Hyperextended with the chin pointing upward toward the ceiling
Rotated 90 degrees to one side
Flexed forward with the chin against the chest
Neutral or sniffing position so the external ear canal is level with the top of the shoulder

explanations.a: Hyperextending an infant's neck can collapse the soft trachea and block the airway.
explanations.b: Rotating the head 90 degrees does not open the airway.
explanations.c: Forward neck flexion closes rather than opens the airway.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 directs the rescuer to keep the infant's neck in neutral or sniffing position so the external ear canal is level with the top of the infant's shoulder.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: mask sizing mouth nose not eyes not below chin
questions.text: AHA Part 6 instructs the rescuer to choose a mask of appropriate size for bag-mask ventilation of an infant or child. Which sizing criteria matches the manual?

answers.text: The mask must cover only the mouth, leaving the nose uncovered
The mask must cover the eyes for full facial coverage
The mask must extend several inches below the chin
The mask must cover the mouth and nose completely without covering the eyes or extending below the bottom edge of the chin

explanations.a: Leaving the nose uncovered allows air to leak and prevents an effective seal.
explanations.b: Covering the eyes is harmful and not part of mask sizing.
explanations.c: A mask that extends below the chin cannot seal properly.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 specifies the mask must cover the mouth and nose completely without covering the eyes or extending below the bottom edge of the chin.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: less volume force infants children chest rise
questions.text: When providing bag-mask ventilation to an infant or small child, AHA Part 6 cautions about volume and force. Which statement matches the manual?

answers.text: Squeeze the bag fully and quickly to overcome airway resistance
Use the same volume as for adults; the child needs full inflation
Use less volume and force than for adults, just enough to see the chest rise
Provide as much volume as possible to flush carbon dioxide

explanations.a: Forceful rapid squeezing causes gastric inflation and lung trauma.
explanations.b: Adult-volume breaths in an infant overinflate the lungs and risk barotrauma.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 says delivering ventilations to infants or small children requires less volume and force than for adults, while still ensuring enough air to see the chest rise.
explanations.d: Maximum-volume breaths cause hyperinflation and reduce cardiac output rather than improving CO2 clearance.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: EC clamp seal two fingers lift jaw
questions.text: AHA Part 6 describes the technique for holding the bag-mask against an infant's or child's face during ventilation. Which technique is specified?

answers.text: Tape the mask to the cheeks
Use the E-C clamp technique to hold the mask against the face while lifting the jaw
Hold the mask loosely above the face
Pinch the mask edges between two fingers only

explanations.a: Taping the mask is not an AHA-recommended technique.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 instructs use of the E-C clamp technique to hold the mask against the face while lifting the jaw, creating a seal.
explanations.c: Holding the mask above the face does not create a seal at all.
explanations.d: Pinching the edges is unreliable and leaks air around the seal.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: jaw thrust suspected neck injury pediatric
questions.text: You suspect a child has a neck injury after a swimming pool dive. AHA Part 6 recommends which airway maneuver first for a suspected neck injury in a child?

answers.text: Head tilt-chin lift to maximize airway patency
Hyperextend the neck as far as possible
Jaw-thrust maneuver without head extension
Place the child in the recovery position immediately

explanations.a: Head tilt-chin lift extends the neck and may worsen a spinal injury.
explanations.b: Hyperextension would be dangerous with suspected spinal injury.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 says to use the jaw-thrust maneuver if a neck injury is suspected, then switch to head tilt-chin lift if the jaw thrust does not open the airway.
explanations.d: Recovery position is for someone with normal breathing and is not an airway-opening maneuver.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: perfusion oxygenated blood heart arteries tissues
questions.text: AHA Part 6 defines perfusion as it is used in pediatric BLS. Which definition matches?

answers.text: The amount of air the lungs hold during inspiration
The electrical activity recorded on an ECG
The flow of oxygenated blood from the heart through the arteries to the body's tissues
The percent of oxygen bound to hemoglobin in venous blood

explanations.a: Lung volume describes ventilation, not perfusion.
explanations.b: ECG activity is electrical conduction, not blood flow itself.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 defines perfusion as the flow of oxygenated blood from the heart through the arteries to the body's tissues.
explanations.d: Venous oxygen saturation measures oxygen delivery but is not the AHA definition of perfusion.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: cool extremities declining mental status weak pulses mottling
questions.text: You are assessing a child whose pulse is borderline. AHA Part 6 lists specific signs of poor perfusion. Which combination matches?

answers.text: Warm pink extremities and a strong bounding pulse
Brisk capillary refill and an alert, oriented mental state
A respiratory rate of 14 per minute and clear lung sounds
Cool extremities, declining mental status, weak pulses, and pallor progressing to mottling or cyanosis

explanations.a: Warm pink skin with strong pulses indicates good perfusion, not poor perfusion.
explanations.b: Brisk capillary refill with an alert state indicates intact perfusion.
explanations.c: A normal respiratory rate with clear lung sounds is reassuring.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 lists cool extremities, declining mental status, weak pulses, and pale or mottled skin progressing to cyanosis as signs of poor perfusion.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: temperature cool extremities skin pallor mottling cyanosis
questions.text: AHA Part 6 describes four categories of signs assessed when evaluating perfusion in a child. Which set matches the manual?

answers.text: Temperature of extremities, mental status, pulse quality, and skin appearance
Blood pressure reading, respiratory rate, ECG rhythm, and temperature
Pupil size, hearing response, skin temperature only, and grip strength
Oxygen saturation, urine output, heart rate, and lung sounds

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 lists temperature (cool extremities), mental status (declining consciousness), pulses (weak), and skin appearance (pallor, mottling, cyanosis) as the four assessment categories for poor perfusion.
explanations.b: Blood pressure, ECG, and respiratory rate are clinical measurements not listed as the AHA Part 6 poor-perfusion categories.
explanations.c: Pupil size and grip strength are not among the AHA Part 6 perfusion assessment categories.
explanations.d: Urine output and lung sounds are clinical measurements not listed in the AHA Part 6 poor-perfusion categories.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: cyanosis lips nail beds skin blue gray late sign
questions.text: AHA Part 6 lists cyanosis as a sign of poor perfusion. Which description of cyanosis matches the manual?

answers.text: A blue or gray coloring of the lips, nail beds, or skin that appears late in poor perfusion
Redness of the cheeks that appears early
Yellow discoloration of the eyes and skin
Purple discoloration of the palms only

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 describes cyanosis as blue or gray coloring of the lips, nail beds, or skin, appearing as a later sign in the progression of poor perfusion.
explanations.b: Redness of the cheeks would suggest flushing or fever, not poor perfusion.
explanations.c: Yellow discoloration describes jaundice, which relates to liver function, not poor perfusion.
explanations.d: Purple discoloration of the palms is not AHA's description of cyanosis.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: HR less than 60 poor perfusion begin CPR
questions.text: You are providing breaths to a child in respiratory failure. On reassessment, the heart rate is 50 per minute with cool, mottled extremities and continued declining responsiveness despite oxygenation and ventilation. What does the AHA pediatric BLS algorithm direct you to do?

answers.text: Continue ventilations only and do not start chest compressions
Stop all care and reassess after the parents arrive
Wait two more minutes before any change in care
Begin CPR with chest compressions and ventilations

explanations.a: Ventilations alone are insufficient when heart rate is under 60 with signs of poor perfusion despite oxygenation.
explanations.b: Stopping care to wait for family is never the correct algorithm action.
explanations.c: Waiting worsens outcome; the algorithm calls for an immediate change in care.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 directs the rescuer to begin CPR when a child's heart rate is under 60 with signs of poor perfusion despite oxygenation and ventilation.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: 6 beats in 10 seconds equivalent to 60 per minute
questions.text: AHA Part 6 expresses the pediatric bradycardia CPR-trigger threshold in terms a rescuer can count at the bedside. Which equivalent does the manual provide?

answers.text: Heart rate less than 60 per minute, equal to fewer than 6 beats in 10 seconds
Heart rate less than 100 per minute, equal to fewer than 10 beats in 10 seconds
Heart rate less than 30 per minute, equal to fewer than 3 beats in 10 seconds
Heart rate less than 80 per minute, equal to fewer than 8 beats in 10 seconds

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 expresses the bradycardia trigger as fewer than 60 per minute, equal to fewer than 6 beats in 10 seconds.
explanations.b: 100 per minute is well above the threshold the algorithm uses.
explanations.c: 30 per minute is far below the threshold and would describe near-asystole.
explanations.d: 80 per minute is above the AHA-defined threshold of 60.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: despite oxygenation ventilation qualifier
questions.text: AHA Part 6 specifies a key qualifier in the bradycardia trigger: the child must have a heart rate under 60 with signs of poor perfusion 'despite' a specific intervention. What is that intervention?

answers.text: Despite attempting chest compressions for 2 minutes
Despite attempting defibrillation twice
Despite oxygenation and ventilation
Despite administration of epinephrine

explanations.a: The trigger applies before chest compressions begin; it is not after an attempted compression period.
explanations.b: Defibrillation is not the qualifier for the bradycardia-with-poor-perfusion CPR trigger.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 says the trigger for starting CPR is a heart rate under 60 with signs of poor perfusion despite oxygenation and ventilation.
explanations.d: Epinephrine is an ALS medication, not a BLS prerequisite for the trigger.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: step 4a continue breaths reassess above 60
questions.text: A child's heart rate is 70 per minute with adequate perfusion after you provide oxygenation and ventilation. According to AHA Part 6, what is the next action?

answers.text: Start CPR immediately because any heart rate requires compressions
Continue providing breaths, check for a pulse every 2 minutes, and reassess the heart rate
Stop all care and observe
Give a shock with the AED to improve rate

explanations.a: A heart rate of 70 with adequate perfusion does not meet the AHA threshold for starting CPR.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 Step 4a says if the heart rate is not below the threshold, continue providing breaths, check pulse every 2 minutes, and reassess heart rate.
explanations.c: Stopping care abandons the child who still needs ventilatory support.
explanations.d: An AED is used for shockable rhythms in cardiac arrest, not for managing a heart rate of 70 with adequate perfusion.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: unwitnessed peds no device 2 minutes CPR first
questions.text: A lone rescuer finds an unresponsive child whose collapse was unwitnessed, and no mobile device is available. Which sequence does AHA Part 6 recommend?

answers.text: Leave immediately to call for help before any CPR
Provide 2 minutes or 5 cycles of CPR, then leave to activate EMS and get an AED
Hold CPR and await parental consent before any intervention
Provide breaths only and do not perform compressions

explanations.a: Leaving an unwitnessed pediatric arrest victim before any CPR omits the most important early intervention for a respiratory cause.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 directs the lone rescuer at an unwitnessed pediatric collapse without a mobile device to perform 2 minutes or 5 cycles of CPR before leaving to activate EMS and get an AED.
explanations.c: Waiting for parents wastes minutes during which oxygen delivery to the brain is failing.
explanations.d: Breaths-only ignores the compression component required for both respiratory and cardiac arrest.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: witnessed sudden collapse leave for AED return CPR
questions.text: You witness a 7-year-old suddenly collapse. You are alone with no mobile device. According to AHA Part 6, what is the recommended sequence?

answers.text: Perform 5 cycles of CPR before any activation
Immediately leave to activate EMS and retrieve the AED, then come back to start CPR
Stay at the child's side and wait for someone to find you
Continue checking responsiveness and do nothing else

explanations.a: The 5-cycles-first rule applies to unwitnessed collapses, not witnessed sudden collapses.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 directs a lone rescuer who witnesses a child's sudden collapse to leave to activate EMS and get an AED, then return to perform CPR.
explanations.c: Doing nothing while waiting wastes critical minutes.
explanations.d: Repeated responsiveness checks without action do not address cardiac arrest.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: mobile device available call first then CPR
questions.text: A lone rescuer finds an unresponsive infant whose collapse was unwitnessed. Unlike the no-device scenario, the rescuer has a mobile phone. According to AHA guidance, what changes?

answers.text: Nothing changes; always do 5 cycles of CPR first regardless of device availability
The rescuer may call EMS on speakerphone while beginning CPR without having to leave the infant
The rescuer must still leave to find a landline
With a mobile device the rescuer skips the AED step entirely

explanations.a: The 5-cycles-first rule applies only when no mobile device is available and the rescuer must physically leave.
explanations.b: With a mobile phone the lone rescuer can call EMS on speakerphone, begin CPR, and avoid leaving the infant unattended.
explanations.c: A mobile phone eliminates the need to leave; a landline search is not required.
explanations.d: AED retrieval remains part of the algorithm; the mobile device only changes the EMS activation step.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: adult witnessed always activate immediately
questions.text: AHA Part 3 contrasts the witnessed-adult-collapse approach with the witnessed-pediatric approach. Which statement correctly describes the adult rule?

answers.text: For witnessed adult collapse, the lone rescuer always activates EMS and retrieves the AED before starting CPR
For witnessed adult collapse, 5 cycles of CPR are performed before any activation
For witnessed adult collapse, compressions are skipped entirely if the rescuer is alone
For witnessed adult collapse, defibrillation is withheld until ALS arrives

explanations.a: AHA Part 3 directs the lone rescuer at a witnessed adult arrest to activate EMS and retrieve a nearby AED before starting CPR, since ventricular fibrillation is likely and early defibrillation is critical.
explanations.b: The 5-cycles-first rule applies to unwitnessed pediatric collapses without a mobile device, not adult collapses.
explanations.c: Compressions are the cornerstone of BLS; skipping them is never the recommendation.
explanations.d: AEDs are used as soon as available; waiting for ALS to defibrillate wastes time.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: carotid child adult neck
questions.text: You are checking a pulse on an unresponsive 5-year-old during the simultaneous breathing-and-pulse assessment. Which artery does AHA BLS direct you to palpate first?

answers.text: The brachial artery in the upper arm
The dorsalis pedis artery in the foot
The carotid artery in the neck
The radial artery at the wrist

explanations.a: The brachial artery is the recommended pulse-check site for infants, not children.
explanations.b: Dorsalis pedis is not used for cardiac arrest pulse checks.
explanations.c: AHA BLS uses the carotid artery in the neck for pulse checks in adults and children.
explanations.d: The radial pulse can be hard to feel during low cardiac output and is not the BLS-specified site.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: brachial infant inside upper arm midway
questions.text: AHA Part 6 specifies the pulse check site for an infant. Which location matches?

answers.text: The carotid pulse in the neck
The brachial artery on the inside of the upper arm, midway between the elbow and shoulder
The femoral artery only
The dorsalis pedis on the foot

explanations.a: Carotid pulse is used for adults and children; the short infant neck makes it unreliable for infants.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 directs rescuers to feel the brachial pulse on the inside of the upper arm, midway between the elbow and shoulder, for an infant.
explanations.c: The femoral artery is an option for a child but is not the AHA-specified primary site for infants.
explanations.d: Dorsalis pedis is not used in BLS pulse checks at any age.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: femoral child alternate midway hip pubic
questions.text: You are assessing pulse on a 4-year-old in cardiac arrest and the carotid landmark is hard to identify. Which alternative pulse site does AHA Part 6 explicitly allow for a child?

answers.text: The femoral artery in the inner thigh
The temporal artery on the forehead
The popliteal artery behind the knee
The radial artery palpated at the wrist

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 names the femoral artery in the inner thigh — midway between the hip bone and pubic bone — as an alternative to the carotid for children.
explanations.b: The temporal artery is not a BLS pulse-check site.
explanations.c: The popliteal site is not described in BLS pulse-check guidance.
explanations.d: Radial pulse is unreliable in low-flow arrest states and is not listed as a BLS pulse-check site.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: not definitely felt 10 seconds start CPR
questions.text: After 9 seconds of a simultaneous breathing-and-pulse check on an unresponsive child, you have not definitely felt a pulse and the chest is motionless. What does AHA guidance direct you to do?

answers.text: Continue checking the pulse for another full minute
Reposition the child and check again from the beginning
Wait until breathing changes before deciding
Start high-quality CPR beginning with chest compressions

explanations.a: Extending the pulse check past 10 seconds is contrary to AHA guidance and only delays compressions.
explanations.b: Restarting the check delays CPR; once cardiac arrest is recognized, compressions begin without further re-checking.
explanations.c: Waiting for breathing changes is not part of the algorithm; cardiac arrest has already been recognized.
explanations.d: If a pulse is not definitely felt within 10 seconds and the person is not breathing normally, AHA directs the rescuer to start high-quality CPR with compressions.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: agonal gasps sign of cardiac arrest not normal
questions.text: A 4-year-old has slow, irregular gasping sounds with long pauses between them. According to the AHA Provider Manual, what do these gasps represent?

answers.text: A sign of cardiac arrest requiring CPR
Normal sleep breathing that requires no intervention
A reliable indicator that the child is recovering
A sign the child needs only supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula

explanations.a: AHA explicitly states agonal gasps are common in the first few minutes of cardiac arrest and are a sign that CPR is needed.
explanations.b: Sleep breathing is regular and quiet, not the slow irregular gasps with long pauses described in agonal breathing.
explanations.c: Agonal gasping is a sign of arrest, not recovery.
explanations.d: Supplemental oxygen alone does not address pulselessness.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: agonal sounds gasps snorts snores groans forceful weak
questions.text: A trainee asks how agonal breathing sounds and looks in an infant or child so they can recognize it in the field. Which description matches AHA Part 6?

answers.text: Steady, even breaths at 20 to 30 per minute
Gasps, snorts, snores, or groans that may be forceful or weak with time passing between them
Loud, continuous wheezing with each breath
Silent, completely absent chest movement

explanations.a: Steady even breaths describe normal breathing, not agonal gasping.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 describes agonal breathing as gasps, snorts, snores, or groans that may be forceful or weak with pauses between them.
explanations.c: Continuous wheezing suggests bronchospasm rather than the irregular gasps of an arrest.
explanations.d: Completely absent breathing is total apnea, which differs from the irregular gasps that define agonal breathing.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: agonal gasping common first minutes arrest rescuer mistake
questions.text: AHA Part 6 warns about a specific rescuer error related to agonal gasping in cardiac arrest. Which error does the manual describe?

answers.text: Rescuers sometimes mistake agonal breathing for normal breathing and fail to recognize cardiac arrest or initiate CPR
Rescuers often mistake normal breathing for agonal gasping and start unnecessary CPR
Rescuers ignore agonal gasping because it is too loud to be concerning
Agonal gasping is only seen in adults and would never be misidentified in children

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 explicitly warns that rescuers can sometimes mistake agonal breathing for normal breathing and fail to recognize cardiac arrest and initiate CPR.
explanations.b: The more common and dangerous error is the reverse — mistaking agonal for normal, not normal for agonal.
explanations.c: Agonal sounds are distinctive but can be confusing; the manual addresses the recognition challenge, not noise level.
explanations.d: Agonal gasping can occur at any age and is specifically addressed in the pediatric section.

questions.name: Pediatric BLS (Children and Infants)
questions.keyword: gasping not normal breathing sign cardiac arrest initiate CPR
questions.text: AHA Part 6 makes a definitive statement about gasping in the context of cardiac arrest recognition. Which statement matches?

answers.text: Gasping is a reliable indicator of recovery and should be monitored without CPR
Gasping is a normal breathing pattern that should not trigger CPR
Gasping is not normal breathing and is a sign of cardiac arrest
Gasping indicates only mild respiratory distress, not cardiac arrest

explanations.a: Gasping indicates arrest, not recovery.
explanations.b: Gasping is abnormal and AHA states it should trigger CPR initiation.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 states explicitly that gasping is not normal breathing and is a sign of cardiac arrest.
explanations.d: Gasping in an unresponsive person indicates cardiac arrest, not mild respiratory distress.
